title: AI Glossary
note: Definitions are paraphrased summaries; see the source for the original wording.

terms.definition: An attack in which someone covertly interferes with the process of training or distilling a model so that the resulting model is compromised.
AI systems built to act as autonomous or semi-autonomous agents that interpret goals, plan steps, use tools such as browsers, code, or APIs, learn from feedback, and adapt while completing tasks.
The effort to ensure an AI system's goals and behavior match human values, rules, and intentions.
Standardized tests used to measure and compare AI systems on specific tasks such as answering questions, recognizing images, writing code, or following instructions.
The ability to work with AI systems productively and responsibly, combining practical tool skills, critical evaluation of outputs, ethical awareness, and adaptability as the technology changes.
The field concerned with making sure AI systems behave reliably and avoid causing harm, even when they are powerful, widely used, or in unexpected situations.
The combined software, hardware, and computing resources that support every stage of the AI lifecycle.
The end-to-end process of building, deploying, and maintaining an AI system, from data preparation and training through testing and deployment.
A set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task, much like a recipe.
A situation in which many organizations rely on the same or very similar algorithms, AI programs, or training data.
A hypothetical AI system able to learn, reason, and apply knowledge across a broad range of tasks and domains at or above human level.
A network of AI systems or agents that share information and coordinate their actions as a collective.
A term coined in 1955 by Stanford's John McCarthy, who described it as the science and engineering of making intelligent machines.
A neural network technique that lets a model concentrate on the most relevant parts of its input when producing an output.
The use of technology to carry out specific tasks according to explicit, predefined human instructions.
The method by which neural networks learn from errors, working backward through the network to determine which parts contributed to the mistake.
Graphical models that use probabilities to show how variables influence one another, like a map of cause and effect.
A tendency of an AI system to produce results that favor or discriminate against certain groups of people.
Datasets so large that traditional data-processing tools cannot handle them, often analyzed with AI to reveal patterns and trends.
A program that simulates conversation with people through text or voice.
Software, also called proprietary software, whose code is restricted and not available for the public to view, modify, or use.
A field of AI that enables computers to interpret and understand images and video.
The amount of input, such as text, that an AI model can take in and consider at one time.
A technique where a model learns by comparing similar and dissimilar examples to understand what makes items alike or different.
Expanding a training dataset by creating modified versions of existing data rather than collecting new data.
Finding patterns and trends in large datasets using statistical methods and machine learning.
An attack in which an adversary deliberately inserts, alters, or mislabels data in a model's training set to corrupt its behavior.
A machine learning algorithm that predicts outcomes by asking a series of yes/no questions that split the data until it reaches a conclusion.
A subset of machine learning that uses large, multi-layer neural networks to learn complex patterns from data automatically.
Generative models that create new content, such as images, by learning to add and then remove noise.
Simplifying complex data by reducing the number of variables while keeping the most important information.
Numerical vector representations of words, images, or other objects that capture their meaning or characteristics.
Techniques that combine multiple models, often weak learners, to produce a prediction that is more accurate and robust than any single model.
Designing, developing, and deploying AI in ways that align with human values, fairness, transparency, and societal well-being.
AI programs that imitate the decisions of human experts in a specific domain using a knowledge base and mainly if-then rules.
Methods that make AI decisions and predictions understandable to humans instead of leaving them as opaque black boxes.
Training a model across many decentralized devices or servers that keep their own data locally, so the data never has to be moved.
An approach in which a model learns to handle a new task from only a small number of examples.
Taking a pre-trained model and training it further on data specific to a task or domain.
Large models, often transformers, trained on broad and diverse data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks and applications.
A highly capable, general-purpose AI model at or near the leading edge of AI development.
An architecture of two competing neural networks, a generator and a discriminator, that together produce realistic synthetic data.
AI systems that can create new content such as text, images, music, code, or video.
A family of large language models built on the transformer architecture that generate human-like text from prompts.
A specialized chip, originally made for rendering graphics, that performs many calculations in parallel and is widely used to train and run AI.
Cases where an AI system produces information that is incorrect, misleading, or fabricated but presented as if it were true.
An approach to AI that puts human needs, values, and well-being at the center of development and deployment.
The study and practice of how people operate and engage with computer systems.
An AI setup that builds human feedback or intervention into how the system operates.
A setting whose value is chosen before the learning process of a machine learning model begins.
A large technology company running vast data-center networks that can rapidly scale computing, storage, and cloud services on demand.
When a trained AI model makes predictions or decisions on new data it has not seen before.
The degree to which humans can understand how an AI system reaches its decisions or predictions.
A simple, intuitive algorithm for classification and regression that relies on the closest examples in the data.
A technique in which a smaller student model is trained to imitate the behavior and outputs of a larger, more capable model.
A structured database that represents information as a network of connected entities and their relationships.
An AI system trained on massive amounts of text to understand and generate human-like language.
The practice of managing the full lifecycle of LLM-based applications in production.
A compressed, abstract, lower-dimensional representation of data that captures its essential features and patterns.
A mathematical measure, also called a cost or objective function, of how far a model's predictions are from the correct values.
A branch of AI in which computers learn patterns and make decisions from data instead of following explicitly programmed rules.
Practices combining machine learning, software engineering, and DevOps to deploy, monitor, and maintain ML models reliably in production.
A mathematical model of a sequence of events in which the probability of the next event depends only on the current state, not on past history.
A simplified mathematical or computational representation of a real-world system or relationship, used to make predictions or understand patterns.
The decline in a model's performance over time as real-world data changes from the data it was trained on.
AI systems that can process, understand, and generate several types of data, such as text, images, audio, and video.
A branch of AI focused on enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
A computational model loosely inspired by the human brain, made of interconnected layers of artificial neurons that process and pass along information.
Software whose original design or blueprint is made freely available for anyone to see and use.
An AI model whose weights, code, training data (or a detailed auditable account of it), and tools are available for others to download, run, inspect, reproduce, modify, and improve.
An AI model whose core components, such as its weights, are publicly released so anyone can download it.
A method that improves a machine learning model by adjusting its settings to reduce errors.
When a model memorizes its training data too closely, including errors and random quirks, and so generalizes poorly to new data.
An internal variable of a machine learning model that is learned and adjusted during training.
Using data, statistics, and machine learning to forecast future outcomes or trends.
Crafting instructions, or prompts, carefully to steer language models toward the outputs you want.
A security attack that uses malicious input to trick a large language model into behaving in unintended ways.
An AI system designed to tackle complex problems by producing a logical, step-by-step chain of thought.
A type of machine learning in which an agent improves through trial and error by taking actions in an environment.
The frameworks, principles, and practices that guide the ethical and safe development and deployment of AI.
A technique in which a language model first looks up external, up-to-date information to produce better answers.
A field combining engineering and computer science, increasingly with AI, to design and build machines that perform physical tasks.
Predictable mathematical relationships showing how AI performance improves as model size, data, and computing power grow.
A training method in which a model creates its own puzzles from raw data and learns by solving them.
Working out the meaning of language by examining relationships among words, phrases, and symbols.
The ability to understand and reason about the three-dimensional physical world, including how objects relate, move, and interact.
Training a model on labeled data, meaning examples paired with the correct answers.
Data generated by algorithms or simulations rather than gathered from real-world events.
A container for numbers arranged in multiple dimensions, like a more advanced spreadsheet.
Splitting text into smaller units called tokens, such as words, word pieces, or characters, that language models can process.
Earlier approaches to AI that relied on explicitly programmed rules, logic, and human-defined knowledge rather than learning from data.
The examples, such as text, images, or audio, used to teach a machine learning model a task.
Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for a different but related task.
A neural network architecture that uses attention to relate all parts of its input at once rather than sequentially.
A test proposed by Alan Turing in 1950 of whether a machine can behave intelligently in a way indistinguishable from a human.
Training a model on unlabeled data so it finds patterns and structure on its own.
A database built to store and efficiently search high-dimensional numerical representations of text, images, audio, and other data.
An adaptation of the transformer architecture, originally built for language, to analyze images.
The numerical parameters in a neural network that set the strength of connections between neurons and shape how the model processes information.
A model's ability to perform tasks or recognize categories it was never explicitly trained on, using its general knowledge.
